title: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh (2014) 2 SCC 1
summary: Constitution Bench held that registration of an FIR is mandatory under Section 154 CrPC where the information discloses a cognizable offence, and a preliminary inquiry is permissible only in limited categories. The principle carries into the BNSS regime (Section 173).
text:
Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh, (2014) 2 SCC 1 (Constitution Bench, Supreme Court of India):

Holding: if the information given to the police discloses the commission of a cognizable offence, its registration (First Information Report under Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973) is mandatory, and the police officer has no discretion to investigate first and register later. A preliminary inquiry may be conducted only in limited categories (e.g. matrimonial disputes, commercial offences, medical negligence, corruption cases where the allegation requires verification) solely to ascertain whether a cognizable offence is disclosed.

Directions issued include: (i) FIR registration followed by prompt investigation; (ii) a copy of the FIR to be given free of cost; (iii) action against officers who refuse to register without justification; (iv) remedies for the informant including approaching the Superintendent of Police under Section 154(3) CrPC and thereafter the Magistrate.

Relevance today: the successor provision in the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Section 173) embodies the same registration obligation; the judgment is the primary authority a citizen can cite when a police station declines to register a complaint disclosing a cognizable offence.

title: Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta (1994) 1 SCC 243
summary: The Supreme Court held that a consumer harassed by a housing authority's deficiency in service is entitled to compensation for harassment and mental agony, payable personally by erring officials — expanding consumer compensation beyond out-of-pocket loss.
text:
Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta, (1994) 1 SCC 243 (Supreme Court of India):

Context: a flat allottee faced prolonged delay and deficiency by the Lucknow Development Authority; the question was whether the consumer fora could award compensation for harassment and mental agony.

Holding: service provided by a statutory authority like a development authority is 'service' under the Consumer Protection Act, and a consumer subjected to deficiency in service is entitled not only to refund of excess payments but also to compensation for harassment, mental agony and oppression. The Court directed that compensation should ordinarily be recovered personally from officials responsible for the harassment, to instil accountability in public administration.

Relevance: foundational authority for claiming compensation for harassment/mental agony in consumer disputes — cited routinely by consumer commissions while awarding compensation under the Consumer Protection Act (1986 then; 2019 now).

title: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) 1 SCC 416
summary: The Supreme Court laid down mandatory requirements for arrest and detention — arrest memoranda, right to inform a friend/relative, medical examination, detention records — to protect against custodial abuse; violations render officials liable and can ground habeas corpus and compensation claims.
text:
D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal, (1997) 1 SCC 416 (Supreme Court of India):

The Court issued binding requirements to be followed in all cases of arrest and detention, including: (i) police personnel carrying clear identification and name tags; (ii) a memo of arrest prepared and attested by a witness and countersigned by the arrestee, with the time and place of arrest; (iii) a friend or relative of the arrestee informed of the arrest and place of detention as soon as practicable; (iv) information about the arrest and detention displayed at a conspicuous place in the police station and in the district control room; (v) entry in the police register about the person informed; (vi) the arrestee entitled to meet his lawyer during interrogation, though not throughout; (vii) medical examination of the arrestee every 48 hours and documentation of injuries; (viii) copies of all documents including the arrest memo sent to the Magistrate.

Failure to comply renders the official liable for departmental action and contempt, and can support compensation claims and habeas corpus petitions under Articles 32/226 of the Constitution.

Relevance: the touchstone authority for rights upon arrest/detention; essential knowledge for unlawful-detention emergencies (alongside immediate remedies: police control room, High Court, NALSA 15100).

title: Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation (2009) 6 SCC 121
summary: The Court standardised the methodology for computing compensation in motor accident claims — notional income based on age and income, standard deductions for personal expenses, and application of multiplier tables — the working framework for MACT awards.
text:
Sarla Verma (Smt.) & Ors. v. DTC & Anr., (2009) 6 SCC 121 (Supreme Court of India):

The Court restated the method for calculating compensation under the Motor Vehicles Act in death cases: (i) ascertain the deceased's income; (ii) deduct an amount towards the deceased's personal living expenses (the balance being the dependency of the family); (iii) multiply the annual dependency by a multiplier selected according to the age of the deceased (with the age of the deceased, not the claimants, being the relevant criterion, capped in the table); (iv) add conventional amounts for loss of consortium, funeral expenses and loss of estate.

The judgment harmonised widely varying MACT awards and remains the starting point for assessing fair compensation, subject to later refinements (e.g. National Insurance Co. v. Pranay Sethi (2017) — verify current position before computing a claim).
